title: Canada | OSFI B-13 Technology and Cyber Risk, E-21 Resilience and PIPEDA
tagline: Spot the lure, raise the alarm, protect customer data and keep critical operations running the way OSFI and PIPEDA expect.
description:
This quest teaches staff of Canadian federally regulated banks how cyber security, operational resilience and privacy fit together under the rules that apply to them: OSFI's **Guideline B-13 Technology and Cyber Risk Management** (effective 1 January 2024), OSFI's **Technology and Cyber Security Incident Reporting Advisory**, OSFI's **Guideline E-21 Operational Risk Management and Resilience** (full adherence expected by 1 September 2026), OSFI's **Guideline B-10 Third-Party Risk Management** and the **Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA)** with its Breach of Security Safeguards Regulations.

B-13 expects banks to make employees aware of the cyber attacks aimed at them, to encourage reporting of suspicious activity and to test staff regularly. E-21 expects adequate training on operational risk, resilience and business continuity plans, and PIPEDA requires staff training on privacy policies and awareness of confidentiality. Every employee, contractor and manager with system access should take it; incident, privacy, resilience and vendor teams get deeper material.

Across five stages you follow a fictional team at Boreal Harbour Bank through phishing lures, OSFI incident reports, privacy breach decisions, critical operations and third parties.

This quest builds knowledge of the guidelines and the law; it does not replace your institution's own policies, procedures or advice from your security, privacy and compliance teams.
audience: All employees and contractors of Canadian federally regulated banks who use the bank's systems or data
Contact centre, branch and payments staff who face phishing, vishing and impersonation attempts
Technology, cyber security and incident response teams who prepare reports to OSFI
Privacy office staff and managers of customer data who handle breaches under PIPEDA
Operational risk, business continuity and vendor management staff working under E-21 and B-10
outcomes: Explain what OSFI Guideline B-13 expects of a bank's technology and cyber governance, operations and security, including awareness and testing of staff
Recognise phishing, vishing and impersonation attempts, including scams that misuse OSFI's name, and report them through the right channel
Decide when a technology or cyber incident is reportable to OSFI and what the initial report and follow-up updates must contain
Apply PIPEDA's accountability and safeguards principles and its breach reporting, notification and record-keeping duties
Describe E-21's critical operations, tolerances for disruption, business continuity training and B-10's third-party life cycle
Show how training, testing, records and reporting prove the bank meets OSFI's and PIPEDA's expectations

quest.name: The Boreal Harbour Firewall
quest.premise: You have just joined the cyber and resilience office of Boreal Harbour Bank, a fictional federally regulated bank headquartered in Toronto with operations in Montréal, Calgary and Halifax. With CISO Ananya Krishnan, resilience head Marc-André Lefebvre, chief privacy officer Adaeze Okafor, contact centre lead Liam Whitehorse and vendor risk lead Sandra Kowalski, you must turn B-13, E-21, B-10 and PIPEDA into everyday decisions.

badge.name: Boreal Harbour Firewall Keeper
badge.description: Awarded for working knowledge of OSFI B-13, the OSFI incident reporting advisory, E-21, B-10 and PIPEDA's safeguard and breach duties.

sessions.title: The OSFI rulebook: B-13 and who owns technology and cyber risk
sessions.summary: Who OSFI supervises, how Guideline B-13 is built around three domains and outcomes, who is accountable for technology and cyber risk, and why awareness and training sit inside the governance domain.
objectives: Explain which institutions Guideline B-13 applies to and when it took effect
Name B-13's three domains and the outcome each one aims for
Describe Senior Management's accountability and the structure, resources and training B-13 expects
Link the risk management framework, risk appetite and culture of risk awareness to everyday staff behaviour

cards.title: Day one in the watchtower
cards.setting: Cyber and resilience office, Boreal Harbour Bank head office, Toronto. 8:15 am, Monday.

lines.text: Your badge works, your laptop asks for a second factor, and a calendar invite already waits: 'B-13 walk-through, 9:00, Ananya.'
Welcome. I'm Ananya Krishnan, CISO. You picked a good week: OSFI's supervisors want to see how we meet Guideline B-13.
Liam Whitehorse, contact centre in Calgary. Honest question: is B-13 an IT thing? My team takes calls, we don't patch servers.
That's the question everyone asks. B-13 covers governance, operations and security, and one part is all about people: awareness, reporting and testing staff like yours.
Marc-André Lefebvre, resilience. And when something breaks, B-13 hands over to E-21 and to OSFI's incident advisory. They fit together.
Stage one is the Watchtower: who OSFI is, what B-13 asks and who owns the risk. Let's climb.

scenes.heading: The supervisor
scenes.narration: OSFI is the prudential supervisor of federally regulated financial institutions, including banks and foreign bank branches. It publishes guidelines that set out what it expects for sound business practices.

scenes.heading: The guideline
scenes.narration: Guideline B-13 sets OSFI's expectations for technology and cyber risk management. OSFI released the final version in July 2022 and it took effect on 1 January 2024.

scenes.heading: Risk based
scenes.narration: B-13 is principles based. There is no one-size-fits-all approach: a bank applies it according to its size, the nature and complexity of its operations and its risk profile.

scenes.heading: Three domains
scenes.narration: The guideline is organised in three domains: governance and risk management, technology operations and resilience, and cyber security. Each domain has a desired outcome.

scenes.heading: People inside
scenes.narration: Training and awareness run through it: a resourced structure with the right expertise and training, a culture of risk awareness, and staff whose cyber awareness is promoted and regularly tested.

cards.title: B-13's three domains and their outcomes
cards.caption: Each domain sets principles and a desired outcome. Read B-13 together with E-21, B-10 and OSFI's incident reporting advisory.

items.label: Governance and risk management
items.right: Risks governed through clear accountabilities and frameworks

items.label: Technology operations and resilience
items.left: Architecture, assets, change, patching, incidents, recovery
items.right: A stable, scalable and resilient technology environment

items.label: Cyber security
items.left: Identify, defend, detect, respond, recover and learn
items.right: Confidentiality, integrity and availability of technology assets

cards.question: Boreal Harbour's Halifax operations team says B-13 does not apply to them because they only run branch services. Who does B-13 apply to?
options: All federally regulated financial institutions, including foreign bank branches, applied on a risk basis
Only the bank's technology department and its outsourced data centres
Only banks that have reported a cyber incident to OSFI in the past
cards.explanation: B-13 applies to all federally regulated financial institutions, including foreign bank branches, and is applied according to size, complexity and risk profile. It sets expectations for the institution as a whole, not just the IT team.

cards.title: Who owns technology and cyber risk
cards.body:
B-13 opens with accountability. Its first principle says **Senior Management** should assign responsibility for technology and cyber risk to senior officers and make sure the structure and resources are adequate.

- **Accountable roles:** examples include the head of IT, the CTO, the CIO and the head of cyber security or **CISO**. These roles should have stature and visibility across the bank.
- **Structure, resources and training (1.1.2):** clear roles, enough people and money, and **appropriate subject-matter expertise and training**.
- **Senior understanding:** Senior Management should include people who understand technology and cyber risk well enough to challenge it.
- **Culture:** the bank should promote a **culture of risk awareness** about technology and cyber risk throughout the institution.

OSFI's Corporate Governance Guideline covers the board's role in strategy and risk appetite. B-13 focuses on what management builds underneath.

cards.title: Match the B-13 element to what it means
cards.prompt: Link each element of B-13's governance domain to its practical meaning.

pairs.right: Named executives such as the CISO or CIO own technology and cyber risk
A documented plan aligned to business strategy, with measurable goals and risk indicators
Processes to identify, assess, manage, monitor and report on technology and cyber risk
Limits, thresholds and tolerance levels the bank sets for technology and cyber risk
Everyone, not only IT, understands and acts on technology and cyber risk

cards.title: Layers of responsibility at Boreal Harbour
cards.caption: B-13 builds from accountability at the top to awareness at every desk.

items.label: Board of directors
items.detail: Sets strategy and risk appetite; oversees management under the Corporate Governance Guideline

items.label: Senior Management
items.detail: Accountable for directing technology and cyber operations; assigns senior officers

items.label: CISO, CIO and senior officers
items.detail: Own the framework, policies, controls and reporting on technology and cyber risk

items.label: Technology and cyber teams
items.detail: Run operations and defences with the expertise and training B-13 expects

items.label: Every employee and contractor
items.detail: Stays aware, follows policy and reports suspicious cyber activity

cards.title: A question from the board
cards.setting: Video call with the chair of the board risk committee. 11:00 am.

lines.text: The risk committee chair has read a draft of the technology and cyber strategy and has one question for Ananya.
She wants to know how we measure whether our cyber risk is inside appetite. Not how many tools we bought.
B-13's framework expects risk appetite measures such as limits, thresholds and tolerance levels, plus regular reporting to Senior Management on exposures and trends.
And where does my team show up in those numbers?
In phishing test results and in how fast your people report suspicious calls. Awareness is measurable, and B-13 expects us to test it.

cards.title: The budget cut
cards.situation: During planning, a business executive proposes to cut the cyber awareness budget in half and to stop phishing simulations for a year, saying 'our firewall is good enough'. The CISO has to respond before the plan goes to Senior Management.

choices.text: Explain that B-13 expects a culture of risk awareness and regular testing of staff, show the risk data and ask Senior Management to decide with that evidence
choices.outcome: Senior Management sees that awareness and testing are OSFI expectations, sees the measured risk, and keeps a program sized to the bank's risk. The decision is documented.

choices.text: Accept the cut quietly and plan to restore the program after the next OSFI review
choices.outcome: The bank would then fall short of an express B-13 expectation, and nobody with accountability has been told of the risk being accepted.

choices.text: Keep the simulations but drop all awareness content, since testing alone is enough
choices.outcome: Testing without awareness misses half of the expectation: B-13 asks banks to create awareness of attack scenarios and to test it. Partly right.

cards.back: Risk from inadequate, disrupted, failed or misused technology assets, people or processes; B-13 treats cyber risk as part of it.
Something tangible such as hardware, or intangible such as software and data, that needs protection and supports services.
Federally regulated financial institution: banks, foreign bank branches, insurers and trust and loan companies supervised by OSFI.
Building security into systems from the design stage, preferring preventive controls over detective ones.
B-13 is applied in proportion to an institution's size, the complexity of its operations and its risk profile.
