cards.question: Which statement about training in B-13's governance domain is accurate?
options: B-13 sets a fixed number of training hours for every technology employee each year
B-13 leaves all training to the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security
The bank should have adequate people with appropriate subject-matter expertise and training to manage technology and cyber risk
Training is only expected for board members, not for technology staff
cards.explanation: Section 1.1.2 expects an organisational structure with adequate people and financial resources and appropriate subject-matter expertise and training. B-13 does not set a fixed number of hours.

cards.title: Real case: OSFI names integrity and security its top risk
cards.body:
In its **Annual Risk Outlook for fiscal year 2025-2026**, OSFI ranked **integrity and security** as its top risk for the institutions it supervises.

OSFI pointed to geopolitical tension, fast technology change and reliance on complex networks of third parties. It said cyber attacks are constant, and that it was seeing elevated levels of **ransomware, exploited software vulnerabilities and data breaches** worldwide. It also warned that third-party providers can open new channels for cyber attacks and insider threats.

In its 2026-2027 outlook, OSFI said malicious cyber activity remains a significant and evolving threat and that **AI-enabled tools** are increasing the speed and scale of attacks. It planned intelligence-led cyber resilience testing and targeted cyber and technology reviews.

**Lesson:** B-13 is not a paper exercise. The supervisor sees cyber risk as a live threat and checks how banks manage it.

cards.title: Stage 1 take-aways
items: OSFI's Guideline B-13 applies to all federally regulated financial institutions and took effect on 1 January 2024.
B-13 has three domains: governance and risk management, technology operations and resilience, and cyber security.
Senior Management is accountable and assigns technology and cyber risk to senior officers such as the CISO or CIO.
Section 1.1.2 expects adequate people, appropriate expertise and training, and a culture of risk awareness.
A risk management framework with appetite measures lets the bank show whether cyber risk is under control.

cards.prompt: Think about your own role. Which part of B-13 touches your work most: governance, technology operations or cyber security? What would a supervisor expect you personally to know?

quiz.question: Which institutions does OSFI's Guideline B-13 apply to?
options: Only Canada's six largest banks and their foreign subsidiaries
Only payment service providers registered with the Bank of Canada under the federal retail payments law
Only provincially regulated credit unions and caisses populaires
All federally regulated financial institutions, foreign bank branches included
quiz.explanation: B-13 applies to all FRFIs, including foreign bank branches and foreign insurance company branches, to the extent consistent with their legal obligations in Canada. Credit unions regulated by provinces are outside OSFI's guideline.

quiz.question: From what date were federally regulated financial institutions expected to meet final Guideline B-13?
options: 1 September 2026
22 August 2024
1 January 2024
13 August 2021
quiz.explanation: OSFI released final B-13 in July 2022 and made it effective 1 January 2024 to give institutions time to self-assess. 13 August 2021 is the incident advisory date; 2024 and 2026 dates relate to E-21.

quiz.question: Which list correctly names B-13's three domains?
options: Strategy; procurement; internal audit of technology assets
Board oversight; customer privacy; anti-money laundering controls
Identify; protect; detect, with response and recovery left to a separate OSFI guideline on resilience
Governance and risk management; technology operations and resilience; cyber security
quiz.explanation: B-13 is organised into governance and risk management, technology operations and resilience, and cyber security, each with a desired outcome. Identify-defend-detect-respond appears inside the cyber security domain, not as the domains.

quiz.question: A new head of IT at Boreal Harbour asks who B-13 says is accountable for directing the bank's technology and cyber security operations. What is the answer?
options: OSFI's Lead Supervisor, who directs the bank's security team during supervisory reviews
Each employee individually, with no central accountability
The external auditor, which signs off on controls each year
Senior Management, which assigns responsibility to senior officers
quiz.explanation: Under section 1.1.1, Senior Management is accountable and should assign responsibility to senior officers such as the CIO, CTO or CISO. OSFI supervises but does not run the bank's operations.

quiz.question: Section 1.1.2 of B-13 expects an appropriate structure, resources and training. Which practice best meets it?
options: Relying on the expertise of the bank's technology vendors and giving the internal security staff no training
Clear cyber roles, enough staff and budget, relevant expertise and ongoing training
Hiring certified staff once and assuming their skills stay current
A single security analyst covering all systems so that costs stay low
quiz.explanation: 1.1.2 asks for clear roles, adequate people and financial resources, appropriate subject-matter expertise and training. Hiring once without ongoing training does not keep expertise appropriate as threats change.

quiz.question: Why does B-13 expect Senior Management to include people with sufficient understanding of technology and cyber risks?
options: So management can understand, challenge and decide on those risks
So that the bank can skip having a dedicated CISO role
Because OSFI must approve each executive's technical certification
So that executives can personally configure firewalls and servers during a serious cyber incident
quiz.explanation: The expectation is about informed oversight: leaders who understand the risk can challenge proposals and decisions. B-13 does not require OSFI to certify executives or let a bank drop a CISO.

quiz.question: Boreal Harbour's technology and cyber risk framework lists limits, thresholds and tolerance levels. Which framework element are these?
options: The cyber incident taxonomy
The software development life cycle
Risk appetite and its measurement
The technology asset inventory
quiz.explanation: B-13 section 1.3.2 lists technology and cyber risk appetite and measurement, such as limits, thresholds and tolerance levels, as an element of the framework. The taxonomy classifies incidents, not appetite.

quiz.question: An executive argues that B-13 forces every bank to buy the same set of security tools. Why is that wrong?
options: B-13 lists approved vendors that each bank must choose from
B-13 only applies to banks that run their own data centres
B-13 is principles based and applied in proportion to each bank's size, complexity and risk profile
B-13 lets each bank opt out if its board approves a waiver
quiz.explanation: OSFI states there is no one-size-fits-all approach; B-13 is read and applied from a risk-based perspective. It names no approved vendors and has no board opt-out.

quiz.question: In its Annual Risk Outlook for fiscal year 2025-2026, how did OSFI rank integrity and security risk?
options: As a risk OSFI would leave entirely to the RCMP to monitor
As its top risk, citing constant cyber attacks and third-party channels
As a minor risk, ranked below every credit, market and liquidity risk that OSFI tracks for banks
As a risk for insurers only, not for deposit-taking banks
quiz.explanation: OSFI's 2025-2026 outlook made integrity and security its top priority and cited ransomware, exploited vulnerabilities, data breaches and third parties. It did not limit the risk to insurers.

quiz.question: Which outcome does B-13 set for its cyber security domain?
options: Annual certification of every bank system by the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security before it goes live
Full outsourcing of security operations to a qualified third party
A secure posture that keeps technology assets confidential, intact and available
A technology environment with no incidents of any kind during the year
quiz.explanation: The cyber security domain's outcome is a secure posture maintaining confidentiality, integrity and availability. B-13 assumes incidents can happen and expects the bank to respond and learn.

sessions.title: Phishing, social engineering and the awareness B-13 expects
sessions.summary: How attackers target employees, customers and third parties by email, phone and text, what B-13 section 3.1.7 expects of awareness, reporting and testing, and how identity and access controls back people up.
objectives: Recognise the warning signs of phishing, vishing, smishing and impersonation, including scams that misuse OSFI's name
Explain the three parts of B-13 section 3.1.7: encourage reporting, create awareness and regularly test employees
Respond correctly to a suspicious email or call and report it through the bank's channel
Describe how multi-factor authentication, least privilege and access attestation support awareness

cards.title: The call that sounded official
cards.setting: Contact centre floor, Boreal Harbour Bank, Calgary. 2:40 pm.

lines.text: One of my agents just took a call from someone who said he was from OSFI. He wanted a list of customers flagged in last week's outage, 'for a regulatory review'.
Did the number look real?
It showed an Ottawa number. My agent nearly started reading names before she paused and called me.
She did exactly the right thing. OSFI itself warns that people impersonate its staff and even spoof its real phone numbers.
Adaeze Okafor, privacy. And reading customer names to an unverified caller would have been a disclosure we'd have to assess as a possible breach.
Welcome to the Lure Lagoon. Today we learn to spot the bait, and why B-13 expects us to test that skill.

scenes.heading: Encourage reporting
scenes.narration: B-13 expects a bank to enable and encourage employees, customers and third parties to report suspicious cyber activity, because each of them can help stop an attack.

scenes.heading: Create awareness
scenes.narration: The bank should make people aware of the attack scenarios aimed directly at them: employees, customers and relevant third parties, not just the IT team.

scenes.heading: Test regularly
scenes.narration: The bank should regularly test its employees to assess their awareness of cyber threats, and test whether the reporting processes and tools actually work.

scenes.heading: Learn and adjust
scenes.narration: Test results show which teams and lures need more attention. The program changes as attackers change their methods.

cards.title: How a social engineering attack narrows in
cards.caption: Each stage is a chance to stop the attack. Most social engineering is stopped at the lure by an alert, trained person.

items.label: Research
items.detail: Attacker gathers names, roles and news from public sources and past breaches

items.label: Lure
items.detail: A message or call that borrows authority, urgency or a trusted brand

items.label: Hook
items.detail: A click, a password, a one-time code or a data disclosure

items.label: Foothold
items.detail: Access to an account, mailbox or system inside the bank

items.label: Objective
items.detail: Fraudulent payment, data theft, ransomware or extortion

cards.title: Red flag or routine?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation: is it a red flag to stop and report, or a routine request you can handle normally?

items.text: A caller says he is from OSFI and asks for a customer list by phone
An email from the 'CEO' asks you to buy gift cards urgently and keep it quiet
A supplier emails new bank details for its next invoice payment
A text asks you to confirm your network password through a link
A customer calls the published number and passes the bank's verification steps
IT announces a planned password change on the intranet, with no link to click
A colleague asks you to share your one-time code so she can 'test' a login
Your manager books a phishing awareness module for your team

cards.question: Which group does B-13 section 3.1.7 expect the bank to make aware of attack scenarios aimed at them?
options: Employees, customers and relevant third parties
Only employees with administrator rights
Only the board and Senior Management
Only customers who use online banking
cards.explanation: Section 3.1.7 covers attack scenarios targeting employees, customers and relevant third parties, and asks the bank to encourage all of them to report suspicious activity.

cards.title: The usual lures and how to beat them
cards.body:
- **Phishing:** an email that imitates a colleague, supplier or regulator and pushes you to click, open or sign in. Check the real sender address and hover over links.
- **Vishing:** a phone call, often with a spoofed caller ID. Hang up and call back on a number you find yourself.
- **Smishing:** a text message with a link or a callback number. Do not use the link.
- **Business email compromise:** a real or look-alike mailbox asks to change payment details or rush a transfer. Verify by a known channel before any change.
- **Pretexting:** a believable story ('I'm from OSFI', 'I'm the new auditor') to get data or access.

**The pause test:** authority + urgency + secrecy + an unusual request = stop. Verify through a channel you control, then **report** through the bank's reporting button or desk, even if you did not fall for it.

cards.title: Real case: fraudsters impersonating OSFI
cards.body:
OSFI's own **Scams and fraud** page warns that some people try to obtain personal information from **financial institutions and members of the public** by claiming to be OSFI employees. It also reports that **legitimate OSFI telephone numbers have been spoofed** to call Canadians as part of other scams.

OSFI states that it **does not ask for personal or confidential information by telephone, email or fax**, and that it does not ask people to pay fees to unlock their funds. It urges anyone contacted this way to report it to the **Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre**, run jointly by the RCMP, the Competition Bureau and the Ontario Provincial Police.

**Lesson for bank staff:** a regulator's name and a real-looking number prove nothing. Requests for customer data from any 'regulator' go through the bank's compliance or regulatory affairs team, never through a cold call to the front line.

cards.title: The test results
cards.setting: Cyber awareness review, Toronto. Thursday morning.

lines.text: Last quarter's phishing simulation: the click rate dropped, but only a third of people who spotted the email reported it.
So people delete it and move on. They think spotting it is enough.
That's the gap. B-13 asks us to test awareness and the effectiveness of reporting processes and tools. A deleted phish helps nobody else.
Sandra Kowalski, third-party risk. Our call-centre vendor's staff never get these tests. Should they?
Section 3.1.7 names relevant third parties for awareness. Let's agree how they take part through the contract.

cards.title: The urgent invoice
cards.situation: Sandra receives an email that looks like it comes from a long-standing IT supplier. It says the supplier has changed banks and asks that today's invoice of CAD 184,000 be paid to a new account. The email is polite, uses the right invoice number, and the sender address has one letter swapped.

choices.text: Do not reply to the email; call the supplier on the number held in the vendor file, report the email through the phishing button and alert accounts payable
choices.outcome: The supplier confirms it has not changed banks. The security team blocks the look-alike domain and warns finance. This is the response B-13's reporting culture is built for.

choices.text: Reply to the email asking for a signed letter on the supplier's letterhead before paying
choices.outcome: The attacker controls that mailbox and sends a convincing letter. Verification must use a channel you already trust, not the suspicious one.

choices.text: Hold the payment for a day but tell nobody, in case it turns out to be genuine
choices.outcome: The payment is safe for now, but the security team never learns about the domain, and colleagues may get the same email. Partly right.

cards.title: Match the control to the attack it blunts
cards.prompt: Link each control from B-13's identity and access expectations to the risk it reduces.

pairs.right: A stolen password alone is not enough to sign in
A compromised account can reach only what that job needs
Old or excess access is found and removed

pairs.left: Privileged credentials in a secure vault
pairs.right: Administrator passwords are not stored where attackers can find them
Unusual sign-ins are spotted and investigated quickly

cards.title: The awareness program loop
cards.caption: B-13 expects awareness to be promoted and regularly tested, so the loop never stops.

items.label: Assess
items.detail: Use threat intelligence to choose the scenarios aimed at your staff, customers and vendors

items.label: Educate
items.detail: Short, role-based training on those scenarios and how to report

items.label: Test
items.detail: Simulations and checks of awareness and of the reporting tools

items.label: Measure
items.detail: Report rates, click rates and time to report by team

items.label: Improve
items.detail: Target weak spots and update content as attacks change

cards.front: Myth: if I delete a phishing email, I've done my job.
cards.back: Fact: report it. Reporting warns the security team and protects colleagues who got the same message.

cards.front: Myth: a caller ID showing a government number is proof.
cards.back: Fact: numbers can be spoofed. OSFI says its own numbers have been spoofed by scammers.

cards.front: Myth: MFA makes awareness training unnecessary.
cards.back: Fact: attackers trick people into reading out one-time codes. Controls and awareness work together.

cards.front: Myth: phishing tests are only about catching people out.
cards.back: Fact: B-13 expects testing to measure awareness and whether reporting tools work, so the bank can improve.

cards.front: Myth: OSFI may call the front line for customer lists.
cards.back: Fact: OSFI says it does not ask for personal or confidential information by phone, email or fax.

cards.question: A phishing simulation shows few clicks but very few reports. Under B-13 section 3.1.7, what does this tell the bank?
options: The program is complete, because a low click rate is the only measure
Awareness is improving, but the effectiveness of reporting processes and tools also needs work
Reporting is optional, so the result needs no action
The bank should stop testing to avoid annoying staff
cards.explanation: Section 3.1.7 expects regular testing of both employees' awareness and the effectiveness of their reporting processes and tools. Low reporting is a gap to fix.

cards.title: Stage 2 take-aways
items: B-13 section 3.1.7: encourage reporting, create awareness of attacks aimed at employees, customers and third parties, and regularly test employees.
Authority, urgency, secrecy and an unusual request together mean stop, verify through your own channel and report.
OSFI warns that scammers impersonate its staff and spoof its numbers; OSFI does not ask for personal information by phone, email or fax.
Payment detail changes are verified with a known contact, never through the message that asked for the change.
MFA, least privilege, access attestation and monitoring back up people; they do not replace awareness.

cards.prompt: Recall the last suspicious message or call you received at work. Did you report it? What would make reporting faster for you and your team?

quiz.question: Which three expectations make up B-13 section 3.1.7 on cyber awareness?
options: Encourage reporting, create awareness of attack scenarios and regularly test employees
Train the board every year, publish a written cyber policy and collect a signed attestation from every member of staff
Hire a vendor, buy filtering software and report click rates to OSFI
Block personal email, ban USB devices and lock screens after one minute
quiz.explanation: Section 3.1.7 asks the bank to enable and encourage reporting, create awareness of attack scenarios aimed at employees, customers and third parties, and regularly test employees' awareness and reporting tools.

quiz.question: A caller with an Ottawa number says he is from OSFI and asks a branch officer for a list of customers affected by an outage. What should the officer do?
options: Email the list to the address the caller provides, for a written record
Ask the caller for his OSFI employee number, then share the list
Read out the list, since OSFI is the bank's supervisor
Decline, take no data, and pass the contact to compliance and the security team as a likely impersonation
quiz.explanation: OSFI warns that people impersonate its employees and spoof real OSFI numbers, and says it does not ask for personal or confidential information by phone, email or fax. An employee number given by the caller proves nothing.

quiz.question: An email from a supplier asks Boreal Harbour to send today's payment to a new account. What is the safest verification?
options: Call the supplier on the number already held in the vendor file
Reply to the email and ask the supplier to confirm
Check that the invoice number in the email is correct
Call the phone number shown in the signature block of the new email to confirm the change
quiz.explanation: Verification must use a channel the bank already trusts. A reply or the number in the suspicious email may reach the attacker, and a correct invoice number can come from a compromised mailbox.

quiz.question: Why does B-13 expect the bank to test the effectiveness of reporting processes and tools, not only employees' awareness?
options: Because tests of tools are cheaper than tests of people
Because spotting an attack helps only if responders hear about it fast
Because OSFI scores the design of each bank's phishing report button during its supervisory reviews
Because reporting tools replace the need for training
quiz.explanation: Reports let the security team block a campaign and warn others. B-13 links awareness to working reporting processes and tools; it does not grade button design.

quiz.question: Which message shows the classic social engineering pattern of authority, urgency and secrecy?
options: 'IT will update laptops on Saturday; no action is needed from you'
'Your training module is due next month in the learning portal'
'This is the CEO. I need gift cards bought within the hour; don't tell anyone'
'The branch will open late on Monday because of the holiday'
quiz.explanation: The CEO message combines a claim of authority, time pressure and a request for secrecy plus an unusual payment method. The other messages are routine notices that ask for nothing risky.

quiz.question: A colleague asks you to read out the one-time code your phone just received so she can 'finish setting up your account'. What is the right response?
options: Share it only if she is in your own department
Share it, because one-time codes expire within minutes and so carry no real risk to the account
Refuse, since the code defeats MFA, and report the request
Share it, then change your password the next day
quiz.explanation: One-time codes are a factor of authentication; anyone who has it can complete a sign-in. Attackers often ask for codes by posing as colleagues or IT. Expiry does not help if the code is used at once.

quiz.question: Which control does B-13 list among identity and access expectations to limit the damage from a compromised employee account?
options: Sharing one service password across the team for convenience
Turning off logging to reduce storage costs
Enforcing least privilege so each account has only the access its role needs
Giving all staff administrator rights so they can fix problems on their own machines without waiting
quiz.explanation: B-13 section 3.2.7 suggests least privilege, regular access attestation, MFA, secure vaulting of privileged credentials and logging and monitoring. Broad admin rights and shared passwords widen the damage.

quiz.question: Boreal Harbour's call-centre vendor handles customer calls. Under B-13 section 3.1.7, how should the vendor's staff be treated?
options: As customers who should receive the bank's marketing alerts
As relevant third parties to make aware and encourage to report
As OSFI's direct responsibility rather than the bank's
As outside B-13 entirely, since they are not bank employees and work under their own employer's policies
quiz.explanation: Section 3.1.7 names relevant third parties alongside employees and customers. The bank uses its contract and oversight to bring them into awareness and reporting.

quiz.question: After a phishing test, the security team learns that one team clicked twice as often as others. What is the best next step under the awareness loop?
options: Discipline every person who clicked and end the program
Report the names of the team members who clicked to OSFI's Technology Risk Division as a cyber incident
Give that team targeted training on the lures it fell for and test again later
Stop testing that team so that results look better
quiz.explanation: Testing exists to find and fix weak spots. Targeted education and retesting improve awareness; hiding results or punishing everyone discourages reporting. Phishing tests are not reported to OSFI as incidents.

quiz.question: Where does OSFI tell people to report scam contacts that falsely use OSFI's name?
options: The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre
The Bank of Canada's payments desk
The Office of the Superintendent's legal department
The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada
quiz.explanation: OSFI's Scams and fraud page urges people to report such contacts to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre, jointly managed by the RCMP, the Competition Bureau and the Ontario Provincial Police. Inside a bank, staff also report to their security team.

sessions.title: Incidents: detect, respond and report to OSFI within 24 hours
sessions.summary: How B-13 expects incidents to be detected, classified, contained and learned from, which technology and cyber incidents OSFI's advisory treats as reportable, and how the initial report and follow-up updates work.
objectives: Describe B-13's expectations for incident management, detection, triage, response and root cause analysis
Apply the characteristics in OSFI's advisory to decide whether an incident is reportable
State who receives an OSFI incident report, in what form and within what time
Explain follow-up updates, the post-incident review and the consequences of failing to report

cards.title: Friday night, 11:52 pm
cards.setting: Security operations centre, Toronto, on a video bridge with the on-call team.

lines.text: Alerts light up: thousands of failed logins to online banking from a botnet, and some customer accounts locked or taken over.
Our controls are blocking most attempts, but not all. Several customers report money moved out.
Is this an OSFI report? It's almost midnight on a Friday.
The advisory says reportable incidents go to OSFI within 24 hours, or sooner if possible. The clock doesn't stop for the weekend.
And if customer information was compromised, I need to start the PIPEDA assessment too. Two different duties, one incident.
Light the signal fire. Let's work out what we report, to whom and when.

scenes.heading: Detect
scenes.narration: B-13 expects continuous security logging and monitoring so malicious or unauthorised activity is spotted and alerts are raised.

scenes.heading: Triage and classify
scenes.narration: High-risk alerts are triaged quickly. Incidents are classified by priority and severity using the bank's cyber incident taxonomy.

scenes.heading: Respond and contain
scenes.narration: A cyber incident response team, available on a continuous basis, contains and recovers, using playbooks aligned with crisis and communication protocols.

scenes.heading: Report
scenes.narration: If the incident is reportable under OSFI's advisory, the bank tells OSFI's Technology Risk Division and its Lead Supervisor in writing within 24 hours, or sooner.

scenes.heading: Learn
scenes.narration: For high-severity incidents, the bank assesses impacts and does root cause analysis, then reports its post-incident review and lessons learned to OSFI.

cards.title: OSFI incident reporting, step by step
cards.caption: If electronic notice is not possible, the advisory allows a phone call followed by a paper submission.

items.label: Assess against criteria
items.detail: Use the advisory's characteristics and the bank's severity levels

items.label: Initial report
items.detail: Within 24 hours or sooner, in writing, to the Technology Risk Division and Lead Supervisor

items.label: Use the form
items.detail: OSFI's technology and cyber incident reporting form; say 'information not yet available' where needed

items.label: Regular updates
items.detail: For example daily, until all details are provided and the incident is contained

items.label: Post-incident review
items.detail: After closure, report the review and lessons learned

cards.title: Reportable to OSFI?
cards.prompt: Using the characteristics in OSFI's advisory, sort each incident.

items.text: Disaster recovery plans activated after a data centre failure
A material vendor tells the bank it is investigating a breach that may touch bank data
A credible extortion threat to launch a DDoS attack on online banking
An incident the bank has also reported to the Privacy Commissioner
An incident rated priority 1 under the bank's own severity scale
A single phishing email blocked by the filter, with no click
A planned weekend maintenance window completed on schedule
A cyber insurance claim has been opened for the event

cards.question: Under OSFI's advisory, who must Boreal Harbour notify of a reportable technology or cyber incident?
options: OSFI's Technology Risk Division and the bank's Lead Supervisor at OSFI
Only the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security
Only the bank's external auditor
Only the Lead Supervisor, by phone, with nothing in writing
cards.explanation: The advisory requires written notice to both the Technology Risk Division and the Lead Supervisor, using OSFI's reporting form. Phone followed by paper is a fallback only when electronic means are unavailable.

cards.title: What makes an incident reportable
The vendor's late-night email
cards.setting: Third-party risk desk, Halifax. Saturday, 7:30 am.

lines.text: Our cloud payroll provider just emailed. They're investigating a breach and can't say yet if our data was touched.
The advisory's own examples include exactly this: a material third party is breached and impact to our data is possible.
Our contract requires them to notify us and give incident details we need for OSFI. B-10 expects that clause.
Good. We report what we know now, mark the rest 'information not yet available', give our best estimates and say when we expect more.

cards.title: Report now or wait for certainty?
cards.situation: At 9:00 am Saturday, Boreal Harbour's incident team confirms account takeovers from the botnet campaign. Some customers are locked out and the controls are failing to block new techniques. The head of digital wants to wait until Monday's root cause analysis before telling OSFI, 'so the report is complete'.

choices.text: Send the written initial report to the Technology Risk Division and Lead Supervisor now, mark unknown details 'information not yet available' with best estimates, and plan daily updates
choices.outcome: OSFI gets timely notice within 24 hours, knows what is still unknown and when more will come. This is what the advisory requires.

choices.text: Wait until Monday so the first report includes the full root cause
choices.outcome: By Monday the 24-hour window has passed. The advisory expects early notice with best estimates, not a complete report. Failing to report can lead to closer supervisory oversight.

choices.text: Phone the Lead Supervisor informally now and send nothing in writing until the root cause is known
choices.outcome: A call shows good faith, but the advisory requires written notice to both the Technology Risk Division and the Lead Supervisor. Phone first is only a fallback when electronic means are unavailable. Partly right.

cards.title: Put the reporting life cycle in order
cards.prompt: Arrange the bank's steps for a reportable cyber incident from first to last.
steps: Detect the activity and triage the alert
Classify severity using the bank's incident taxonomy and OSFI's criteria
Send the written initial report within 24 hours, or sooner
Provide regular updates, for example daily, until all details are given
Contain the incident, recover and close it
Report the post-incident review and lessons learned to OSFI

cards.title: Initial report versus follow-up
cards.caption: Depending on severity and speed, OSFI may ask the bank to change the method and frequency of updates.

items.label: Timing
items.left: Within 24 hours, or sooner if possible
items.right: Regular, e.g. daily, or as OSFI asks

items.label: Content
items.left: Known facts plus best estimates; unknowns marked
items.right: New information, remediation actions and plans

items.label: Ends when
items.left: The first written notice is sent
items.right: All details are provided and the incident is resolved

cards.back: The OSFI team that, with the Lead Supervisor, receives technology and cyber incident reports.
The OSFI supervisor assigned to the bank; consult them when unsure whether to report.
The phrase the advisory asks banks to use for details still unknown in the initial report.
B-13's expected classification of incidents by severity, category, type and root cause.
For high-severity incidents, an assessment of weaknesses in people, processes, technology and data.
Possible supervisory consequences OSFI names for failing to report incidents as required.

cards.question: What does OSFI's advisory say may happen if a bank fails to report incidents as required?
options: An automatic fine of a fixed amount per day of delay
Immediate loss of the bank's charter
No consequence, since reporting is voluntary
Increased supervisory oversight, such as enhanced monitoring, watch-listing or staging
cards.explanation: The advisory says failure to report may lead to increased supervisory oversight including enhanced monitoring, watch-listing or staging. It does not set a fixed daily fine.

cards.title: Reporting habits that save hours
cards.body:
- Keep OSFI's reporting form and contacts in the incident playbook, not in one person's inbox.
- Start a timeline at first detection; the 24-hour clock is easier to meet when facts are logged as they happen.
- Flag early when an incident may also be a **PIPEDA breach** so the privacy office runs its assessment in parallel.
- Make sure vendor contracts require timely incident notice and the details OSFI asks for.
- When in doubt, talk to the Lead Supervisor: OSFI encourages precautionary notice.

cards.title: Stage 3 take-aways
items: B-13 expects logging, detection, triage, a continuously available response team, a cyber incident taxonomy and root cause analysis.
A reportable incident may have one or more of the advisory's characteristics; when unsure, notify OSFI as a precaution.
Report in writing to OSFI's Technology Risk Division and the Lead Supervisor within 24 hours, or sooner, using OSFI's form.
Give best estimates, mark unknowns 'information not yet available', update regularly and report the post-incident review.
Failing to report can bring enhanced monitoring, watch-listing or staging; vendor contracts must support the bank's reporting.

cards.prompt: If a serious incident started on your team's systems tonight, who would you call first, and do you know where the bank's incident playbook and OSFI reporting steps are kept?

quiz.question: Within what time must a federally regulated bank report a reportable technology or cyber incident to OSFI under the advisory?
options: Within 10 business days of the incident
As soon as feasible after the board is briefed
Within 24 hours, or sooner if possible
Within 72 hours of confirming the root cause
quiz.explanation: OSFI's advisory requires initial notice within 24 hours, or sooner if possible. 'As soon as feasible' is PIPEDA's wording for breach reports to the Privacy Commissioner, not OSFI's.

quiz.question: Which description matches the advisory's definition of a technology or cyber security incident?
options: Only an attack by an external criminal group that causes financial loss
Only an event that has already been reported to law enforcement
An incident that affects, or could affect, operations, including confidentiality, integrity or availability of systems and information
Only an outage of the core banking system lasting more than a day
quiz.explanation: The definition covers actual or potential impact on operations, including confidentiality, integrity or availability. It is not limited to criminals, long outages or police reports.

quiz.question: At the time of the initial OSFI report, Boreal Harbour does not yet know how many customers are affected. What should the report do?
options: Mark it 'information not yet available', give best estimates and say when more will follow
Delay the report until the number is confirmed
Report zero affected customers until proven otherwise
Leave the field blank and send the report without comment, then correct the record once the number is final
quiz.explanation: The advisory asks banks to indicate 'information not yet available', provide best estimates and all other details, and state when more information is expected. Delay or a guess of zero would mislead.

quiz.question: A material third party tells the bank it was breached and is investigating; the bank's data may be affected. How does OSFI's advisory treat this?
options: It is reportable only after the vendor proves bank data was stolen
It is one of the advisory's examples of a reportable incident
It is the vendor's matter alone and never reportable by the bank
It is reportable only if the vendor is located outside Canada
quiz.explanation: Appendix I of the advisory lists a breach at a material third party, where impact to the bank's data is possible, as an example of a reportable incident. Impact to a third party affecting the bank is also a listed characteristic.

quiz.question: After the initial report, what reporting does the advisory expect while the incident is ongoing?
options: Monthly updates through the bank's regular supervisory meeting, with a written summary at year end
A single update when the media first reports the incident
Regular updates, for example daily, as new information becomes available
No further contact until a final report in 90 days
quiz.explanation: OSFI expects regular updates, such as daily, until all details have been provided, including remediation actions and plans. OSFI may change the method and frequency based on severity.

quiz.question: The bank's email system is down and the incident team cannot send the OSFI form electronically. What does the advisory allow?
options: Waiting until email is restored, however long it takes
Asking the vendor to notify OSFI on the bank's behalf
Posting a notice on the bank's public website instead
Notice by telephone, followed by a paper submission
quiz.explanation: A footnote in the advisory says that if electronic means are not available, telephone notification followed by a paper submission is acceptable. The bank remains responsible for notifying.

quiz.question: Which of these is listed in OSFI's advisory as a characteristic of a reportable incident?
options: The incident was caused by an employee working remotely
The incident affected a test environment that holds no live customer data and no production systems
The incident has been reported to the board of directors or senior management
The incident happened outside normal business hours
quiz.explanation: Reporting to the board or senior executive management is one of the listed characteristics. Time of day, remote work or a test system with no impact are not criteria in themselves.

quiz.question: What does B-13 expect after a high-severity cyber incident?
options: A public apology within 24 hours and no internal review
Dismissal of the staff on duty before any analysis is done
Replacement of every system involved, whatever the cause
A detailed post-incident assessment of impacts with a root cause analysis covering people, processes, technology and data
quiz.explanation: B-13 section 3.4.5 expects a post-incident assessment of direct and indirect impacts and a root cause analysis of weaknesses in people, processes, technology and data, to drive remediation and lessons learned.

quiz.question: Boreal Harbour is unsure whether a moderate outage meets any of OSFI's criteria. What does the advisory suggest?
options: Decide internally not to report, since doubt means it is minor
Consult the Lead Supervisor and notify OSFI as a precaution
Report it only to the Privacy Commissioner instead
Wait to see whether the media picks up the story
quiz.explanation: The advisory says that when in doubt, institutions should consult their Lead Supervisor, and that precautionary notification is encouraged when the criteria do not clearly fit.

quiz.question: Why does B-10 expect contracts with third parties to contain incident notification provisions?
options: So that the vendor reports its incidents directly to OSFI and the bank no longer needs to report them
So the bank can meet its own reporting duties under OSFI's incident advisory
So the bank can recover its costs from the vendor automatically
So that incidents at vendors are kept out of the bank's records
quiz.explanation: B-10 expects written agreements to let the bank comply with OSFI's Technology and Cyber Security Incident Reporting Advisory, including timely notice and incident details. The bank stays accountable for reporting.

sessions.title: PIPEDA: accountability, safeguards and breaches of security safeguards
sessions.summary: How PIPEDA's accountability and safeguards principles apply to bank staff, what counts as a breach of security safeguards, when the Privacy Commissioner and individuals must be told, and what records the bank keeps.
objectives: Explain PIPEDA's accountability principle, including responsibility for data sent to third parties and the duty to train staff
Describe the safeguards principle: physical, organisational and technological measures, staff awareness and careful disposal
Assess whether a breach creates a real risk of significant harm using PIPEDA's definition and factors
State what the report to the Commissioner, the notice to individuals and the breach record must cover

cards.title: The spreadsheet that left the building
cards.setting: Privacy office, Boreal Harbour Bank, Toronto. Tuesday, 10:05 am.

lines.text: A relationship manager emailed a spreadsheet of 2,300 mortgage customers to a personal address so she could work from home. Her personal account was then compromised.
So the data left our systems because of a shortcut, not a hacker breaking in?
Either way, PIPEDA calls it a breach of security safeguards if personal information was lost, accessed or disclosed without authority because safeguards failed or were missing.
Names, income, addresses and loan balances. That's sensitive.
Then the clock is running on our assessment. Welcome to the Vault of Names: today you learn to decide, report, notify and record.

scenes.heading: Accountable
scenes.narration: Under PIPEDA's first principle, the bank is responsible for personal information it controls and names someone accountable for compliance, often the chief privacy officer.

scenes.heading: Safeguarded
scenes.narration: The safeguards principle says personal information must be protected by security safeguards matched to its sensitivity, in any format.

scenes.heading: Assessed
scenes.narration: When safeguards fail, the bank decides whether it is reasonable to believe the breach creates a real risk of significant harm to an individual.

scenes.heading: Reported and recorded
scenes.narration: If it does, the bank reports to the Privacy Commissioner and notifies the people affected. Either way, it records every breach.

cards.title: Accountability and safeguards side by side
cards.caption: PIPEDA Schedule 1, clauses 4.1 and 4.7, in our own words.

items.label: Core idea
items.left: The bank answers for personal data it controls
items.right: Protection matched to how sensitive the data is

items.label: Third parties
items.left: Contracts give comparable protection during processing
items.right: Safeguards apply in any format and location

cards.title: Which kind of safeguard?
cards.prompt: PIPEDA gives three kinds of protection. Sort each measure.

items.text: Locked cabinets for paper loan files
Restricted access to the server room
Need-to-know access to customer records
Background checks for staff with data access
Encryption of customer data on laptops
Strong passwords and multi-factor sign-in
Clean desk rule enforced by branch managers
Data loss prevention that blocks emails to personal accounts

cards.question: A bank sends customer data to a third-party processor. Under PIPEDA's accountability principle, who is responsible for that data?
options: The bank remains responsible and must use contracts or other means to get comparable protection
The processor alone becomes responsible once it receives the data
The Privacy Commissioner becomes responsible for supervising the processor
Nobody, until the customer consents again to the transfer
cards.explanation: Clause 4.1.3 says an organisation is responsible for personal information transferred to a third party for processing and must use contractual or other means to provide comparable protection.

cards.title: Real risk of significant harm
cards.body:
PIPEDA defines a **breach of security safeguards** as the loss of, unauthorised access to or unauthorised disclosure of personal information resulting from a breach of the bank's safeguards, or from a failure to set them up.

**Significant harm** includes bodily harm, humiliation, damage to reputation or relationships, loss of employment, business or professional opportunities, **financial loss, identity theft**, negative effects on the **credit record** and damage to or loss of property.

To judge whether there is a **real risk**, the Act points to:
- the **sensitivity** of the information involved; and
- the **probability** that it has been, is being or will be misused;
- plus any other factor set by regulation.

If it is reasonable to believe there is a real risk of significant harm, the bank must **report to the Commissioner** and **notify affected individuals**, each as soon as feasible after it determines that the breach occurred.

cards.title: Match the duty to its PIPEDA source
cards.prompt: Link each breach duty to what the law requires.

pairs.right: In writing, with prescribed content, as soon as feasible when there is a real risk of significant harm
Directly and conspicuously, with enough to understand the harm and protect themselves
Tell bodies that may reduce or mitigate the harm, such as a credit bureau or police
Record every breach, whether reportable or not, for 24 months
Provide access to, or a copy of, breach records on request

lines.text: Sensitive financial data, and the personal mailbox was taken over by an unknown attacker. Probability of misuse is real.
And because the employee's personal account was the weak point, I'll check whether any bank systems were touched too.
My conclusion: real risk of significant harm. We report to the Commissioner and notify the 2,300 customers directly. And it goes in the breach record.
My contact centre will get calls. What do we tell people?
What happened, when, what data, what we've done, what they can do, and who to contact. The regulations list it all.

cards.title: The misdirected statement
cards.situation: A Montréal branch employee mails one customer's monthly statement to the wrong address. The recipient, a neighbour, calls the next day, says she opened it by mistake, and returns it unread beyond the first page. The statement shows the name, address and account balance.

choices.text: Log the incident with the privacy office, which assesses sensitivity and probability of misuse, records the breach and decides on notification
choices.outcome: The privacy office documents its reasoning. Whatever the outcome on reporting, PIPEDA requires a record of every breach, and the branch fixes the mailing error.

choices.text: Do nothing, since the statement came back and no harm is likely
choices.outcome: Even if the assessment finds no real risk of significant harm, the bank must still keep a record of every breach of security safeguards. Ignoring it breaks that duty.

choices.text: Immediately report it to the Commissioner without any assessment, to be safe
choices.outcome: Reporting is required when there is a real risk of significant harm; skipping the assessment wastes effort and still needs a record. Partly right, because it errs on the side of openness.

cards.title: Breach handling at Boreal Harbour
cards.caption: If the breach is also a technology or cyber incident, OSFI's 24-hour reporting runs in parallel.

items.label: Contain
items.detail: Stop the loss, recover data where possible and preserve evidence

items.label: Escalate
items.detail: Tell the privacy office and security team at once

items.label: Assess
items.detail: Sensitivity plus probability of misuse: real risk of significant harm?

items.label: Report and notify
items.detail: Commissioner, individuals and organisations that can reduce harm

items.label: Record
items.detail: Log every breach and keep the record for 24 months

cards.back: A description of what happened and, if known, the cause.
The number of individuals affected or, if unknown, an approximate number.
What the bank has done to reduce harm, and what the person can do to protect themselves.
Contact details the person can use to learn more about the breach.
Allowed by public communication when direct notice could cause more harm, cause undue hardship or contact details are missing.
Must contain enough information for the Commissioner to verify compliance with reporting and notification duties.

cards.question: A breach is assessed as not creating a real risk of significant harm. What must the bank still do under PIPEDA?
options: Nothing at all, because only reportable breaches matter
Notify every customer of the bank as a precaution
Keep a record of the breach and provide it to the Commissioner on request
Delete all evidence of the breach after 30 days
cards.explanation: Section 10.3 requires a record of every breach of security safeguards, and the Breach of Security Safeguards Regulations require it to be kept for 24 months after the bank determines the breach occurred.

cards.title: Staff habits that stop breaches
cards.body:
- Never send customer data to personal email or cloud accounts.
- Check the address before you mail, email or fax customer information.
- Share data on a need-to-know basis, even inside the bank.
- Lock screens and files; dispose of paper in secure shredding bins.
- Report a possible breach to the privacy office **at once**: the assessment, reporting and notice clocks start when the bank determines the breach has occurred, and fast escalation protects customers.

cards.title: Stage 4 take-aways
items: PIPEDA makes the bank accountable for personal information it controls, including data sent to processors, and expects staff training.
Safeguards must match sensitivity and combine physical, organisational and technological measures; employees must understand confidentiality.
A breach of security safeguards is the loss of, or unauthorised access to or disclosure of, personal information because safeguards failed or were missing.
Where there is a real risk of significant harm, report to the Commissioner and notify individuals as soon as feasible; notify bodies that can reduce harm.
Record every breach for 24 months; knowingly failing to report, notify or keep records is an offence under section 28.

cards.prompt: Which customer data do you handle every day? Name one shortcut you have seen, or been tempted to take, that could turn into a breach of security safeguards.

quiz.question: Under PIPEDA's safeguards principle, what should determine the level of protection given to personal information?
options: The age of the customer, with older and more vulnerable customers always getting more protection
Whether the data is held on paper, which needs no protection
The cost of the safeguard compared with the bank's annual budget
The sensitivity of the information, along with its amount, format and storage
quiz.explanation: Clause 4.7 says safeguards must be appropriate to sensitivity, and 4.7.2 adds amount, distribution, format and storage. Information is protected regardless of format, including paper.

quiz.question: Which of these does PIPEDA give as an example of an organisational safeguard?
options: Limiting access on a need-to-know basis
Requiring strong passwords on all customer accounts
Locked filing cabinets
Encrypting files on laptops
quiz.explanation: Clause 4.7.3 gives security clearances and need-to-know access as organisational measures, locked cabinets as physical, and passwords and encryption as technological measures.

quiz.question: What does PIPEDA's accountability principle say about staff training?
options: Training is optional if the bank has a written privacy policy
Organisations must train staff on, and communicate, their privacy policies and practices
Training must be delivered by the Office of the Privacy Commissioner, not by the organisation itself, every year
Training is needed only for the designated privacy officer
quiz.explanation: Clause 4.1.4(c) requires training staff and communicating information about the organisation's policies and practices. Clause 4.7.4 adds that employees must be aware of the importance of confidentiality.

quiz.question: Which event is a breach of security safeguards under PIPEDA?
options: A customer asks to see the personal information the bank holds about her and how it has been used
A customer withdraws consent to marketing emails
The bank updates its privacy policy and posts it on its website
A laptop holding unencrypted customer data is stolen from an employee's car
quiz.explanation: Loss of personal information resulting from a failure of the bank's safeguards is a breach of security safeguards. Access requests, policy updates and consent withdrawals are not breaches.

quiz.question: Which two factors does PIPEDA name for judging whether a breach creates a real risk of significant harm?
options: The cost of fixing the breach and the bank's insurance cover
The sensitivity of the information and the probability it will be misused
The number of employees involved and the time of day
Whether the media has reported it and whether OSFI was told
quiz.explanation: Section 10.1(8) lists sensitivity and probability of misuse, plus any prescribed factor. Cost, media attention and OSFI reporting are not the legal test.

quiz.question: When must a bank report a breach that creates a real risk of significant harm to the Privacy Commissioner?
options: Only once a customer files a complaint about it
As soon as feasible after the bank determines that the breach has occurred
Within 30 days, after all customers have been notified
Within 24 hours of the breach, under the same timetable as OSFI's technology and cyber incident advisory
quiz.explanation: Section 10.1(2) requires the report as soon as feasible after the organisation determines the breach occurred. The 24-hour deadline belongs to OSFI's separate incident advisory.

quiz.question: Boreal Harbour has no current contact details for 40 former customers affected by a breach. How can it notify them?
options: By waiting until those customers return to a branch
It need not notify them at all because contact is impossible
By asking OSFI to contact them on the bank's behalf
By indirect notice, such as a public communication likely to reach them
quiz.explanation: The Breach of Security Safeguards Regulations allow indirect notice, by public communication or similar measure, when the organisation lacks contact information, when direct notice could cause further harm or would cause undue hardship.

quiz.question: How long must the bank keep its record of a breach of security safeguards?
options: 24 months after the day it determines the breach occurred
Until the Commissioner closes any investigation
6 months after the breach is contained
5 years after the customer relationship ends, in line with the bank's general record retention schedule
quiz.explanation: Section 6 of the Breach of Security Safeguards Regulations requires records of every breach for 24 months after the organisation determines the breach occurred.

quiz.question: Which item must the bank's notice to an affected individual include under the regulations?
options: A copy of the report sent to OSFI
The name of the employee who caused the breach
The bank's total annual spending on security
Steps the individual could take to reduce or mitigate the risk of harm
quiz.explanation: Section 3 of the regulations lists the circumstances, timing, data involved, steps taken by the bank, steps the individual could take and contact information. Naming staff or sharing OSFI reports is not required.

quiz.question: Under section 28 of PIPEDA, which conduct can be an offence?
options: Knowingly failing to report or notify under section 10.1, or to keep breach records
Reporting a breach that later proves to be minor
Keeping breach records for longer than the minimum period set in the Breach of Security Safeguards Regulations
Notifying customers by telephone rather than email
quiz.explanation: Section 28 makes it an offence to knowingly contravene section 10.1 or subsection 10.3(1), among others, with fines up to $10,000 on summary conviction or $100,000 on indictment. Over-reporting is not an offence.

sessions.title: E-21 resilience, B-10 third parties and assessment readiness
sessions.summary: How E-21 frames operational risk and resilience, critical operations, tolerances for disruption, business continuity and data risk, how B-10 governs third parties across their life cycle, and how the bank proves it meets OSFI and PIPEDA expectations.
objectives: Define operational risk, operational resilience, critical operations and tolerance for disruption as E-21 uses them
Explain E-21's training expectations for business and central functions, business continuity plans and data roles
Describe B-10's third-party life cycle and why the bank remains accountable
Assemble the evidence a supervisor or auditor expects: roles, training records, tests, incident and breach records

cards.title: The ice storm drill
cards.setting: Crisis management room, Montréal, with Toronto and Halifax on screen. Wednesday, 9:00 am.

lines.text: Today's exercise: an ice storm knocks out power in Montréal for three days, and our payments vendor's data centre fails over badly.
That vendor supports our retail payments. If it's down, customers can't pay rent.
Retail payments are a critical operation. Our tolerance for disruption says how long we can go before the harm is unacceptable. Let's see if we stay inside it.
And a cyber-attack could cause the same outage. E-21, B-13 and B-10 all meet here.
E-21 also expects staff to be trained on the business continuity plan, including how it is activated. So this drill is training too. Let's begin.

scenes.heading: The guideline
scenes.narration: OSFI published final Guideline E-21 on Operational Risk Management and Resilience on 22 August 2024. Sections 1 and 2 applied at once; full adherence was expected by 1 September 2026.

scenes.heading: Risk and resilience
scenes.narration: Operational risk is the risk of loss from people, inadequate processes and systems, or external events. Operational resilience is the ability to deliver operations, especially critical ones, through disruption.

scenes.heading: Critical operations
scenes.narration: Banks identify their critical operations, map the people, technology, processes, facilities and third parties behind them, and set tolerances for disruption.

scenes.heading: Scenario testing
scenes.narration: Banks test severe but plausible scenarios, such as cyber incidents, technology failures, third-party disruption and natural disasters, to see whether they stay within tolerance.

scenes.heading: Trained people
scenes.narration: Business and central functions should give staff adequate training on operational risk and resilience, staff are trained on continuity plans, and people managing data receive training.

cards.title: Risk appetite versus tolerance for disruption
cards.caption: E-21 keeps the two ideas apart: appetite is about choice in normal times, tolerance is about survival in a crisis.

items.label: Risk appetite
items.detail: Risk the bank willingly accepts to meet business goals

items.label: Operational risk limits
items.detail: Usually set lower than tolerances for disruption

items.label: Tolerance for disruption
items.detail: Maximum disruption the bank can withstand in a crisis

items.label: Scenario testing
items.detail: Checks whether critical operations stay within tolerance

cards.title: Match the E-21 term to its meaning
cards.prompt: Link each E-21 term to the right description.

pairs.right: An unintended outcome from operational risk, including near misses
Services whose disruption would threaten the bank's safety or harm others
The most disruption the bank can withstand under severe but plausible scenarios
A senior group that decides and coordinates during a crisis
Risk of loss from collecting, storing, using, sharing or disposing of data

cards.question: According to the E-21 backgrounder, by when was full adherence to Guideline E-21 expected?
options: 1 September 2026
1 January 2024
13 August 2021
30 April 2023
cards.explanation: E-21 was published on 22 August 2024. Sections 1 and 2 on operational risk management applied immediately, and full adherence was expected by 1 September 2026. 1 January 2024 is B-13's effective date.

cards.title: Training duties in E-21
cards.body:
E-21 makes training part of resilience, not an extra.

- **Section 1.2, business and central functions:** they own operational risk, identify critical operations, escalate events and **provide adequate training to staff on operational risk management and resilience**.
- **Section 4.1.2, business continuity plans:** plans set roles, invocation protocols, backup staff, staff safety, recovery targets and communications, and **staff should be trained on the plans, including how they are activated and how operations run during disruption**.
- **Section 4.1.3, testing:** continuity tests should help senior management and staff understand their roles, and cover long, simultaneous and third-party disruptions.
- **Section 4.7, data risk:** the data risk program should include **training for the people who manage and oversee data**, plus processes for escalating and responding to data breaches.

Senior management is ultimately accountable, and internal audit gives independent assurance that controls work.

lines.text: The payments vendor says its backup site is fine, but its own subcontractor for network links is down too.
Subcontractors are part of B-10. We should have known that dependency when we did due diligence.
We did. Our contract requires them to keep and test continuity plans and to tell us about subcontractor incidents. Now we use the contingency plan.
And remember: we stay accountable. OSFI doesn't accept 'the vendor did it' as an answer.

cards.title: B-10's third-party life cycle
cards.caption: B-10 applies to all third-party arrangements, scaled to risk and criticality; the bank remains accountable throughout.

items.label: Risk assessment
items.detail: Judge risk and criticality before entering and periodically after

items.label: Due diligence
items.detail: Check the third party first and on an ongoing basis, in proportion to risk

items.label: Contract
items.detail: Written rights and duties: data security, audit, continuity, incident notice

items.label: Monitoring
items.detail: Verify performance, financial soundness and incident handling

items.label: Exit or renewal
items.detail: Planned or stressed exit with triggers, or reassess at renewal

cards.title: The new cloud contract
cards.situation: A business unit wants to sign a cloud analytics vendor next week to process customer transaction data. The vendor's standard contract has no audit rights, no incident notice clause and says nothing about subcontractors. The business head says, 'It's only analytics, legal can fix it later.'

choices.text: Pause signing until third-party risk assesses criticality, due diligence is done and the contract covers data security, incident notice, audit rights and subcontractors
choices.outcome: The bank meets B-10's life cycle and PIPEDA's accountability for data sent to processors. Signing later is cheaper than renegotiating after an incident.

choices.text: Sign now and add the missing clauses at the first renewal in three years
choices.outcome: For three years the bank cannot audit the vendor, may not learn of incidents in time to report to OSFI, and has no comparable privacy protection in contract.

choices.text: Sign now but forbid the vendor from receiving any data until the clauses are agreed
choices.outcome: This avoids immediate exposure, but due diligence and the contract gaps remain unresolved and the project stalls with no plan. Partly right.

cards.title: Prepare for a supervisory review
cards.prompt: Put the steps for showing OSFI and auditors your cyber and resilience readiness in a sensible order.
steps: Confirm accountable owners: CISO, privacy officer, operational risk, third-party risk
Map critical operations, dependencies and tolerances for disruption
Gather training records: awareness, role-based, continuity and data training
Collect test evidence: phishing simulations, continuity and scenario tests
Assemble incident reports to OSFI and the PIPEDA breach record
Track remediation of findings and report to senior management and the board

cards.title: Who does what at Boreal Harbour

cards.back: Senior officer for cyber risk under B-13; runs awareness, testing, detection and incident response.
PIPEDA's designated accountable individual; leads breach assessment, Commissioner reports and the breach record.
Coordinates E-21: critical operations, tolerances, continuity plans, scenario tests and training.
Runs B-10's life cycle: risk assessment, due diligence, contracts, monitoring and exit plans.
Gives independent assurance that operational risk controls and processes work as designed.
Completes training, follows policy, protects customer data and reports suspicious activity at once.

cards.title: The numbers this quest has taught
cards.caption: Sources: OSFI's incident advisory, the Breach of Security Safeguards Regulations, OSFI's B-13 news release and E-21 backgrounder.

items.label: OSFI incident report
items.detail: Initial written notice, or sooner if possible

items.label: PIPEDA breach records
items.detail: Kept from the day the breach is determined

items.label: B-13 effective
items.detail: Technology and cyber risk expectations apply

items.label: E-21 full adherence
items.detail: Phased expectations fully in place

cards.question: Which evidence best shows OSFI that the B-13 section 3.1.7 expectation is met?
options: A copy of the security policy signed by the CISO
Records of awareness content, regular phishing tests, reporting rates and follow-up actions
The invoice for the bank's email filtering tool
A list of employees who joined during the year
cards.explanation: Section 3.1.7 asks for awareness, encouraged reporting and regular testing of employees and of reporting tools. Evidence must show those activities and what changed as a result.

cards.title: Real case: OSFI's supervisory plan for 2026-2027
cards.body:
In its **Annual Risk Outlook for fiscal year 2026-2027**, OSFI said malicious cyber activity remains a **significant and evolving threat** to the financial sector and its critical service partners, with threat actors using **advanced and AI-enabled tools** that increase the speed and scale of attacks. It named software vulnerabilities in common technology as the most persistent high-impact technology risk and flagged the **concentration and complexity of third-party providers**.

OSFI said it planned **intelligence-led cyber resilience testing**, targeted cyber and technology risk reviews, monitoring of significant cyber incidents reported to it, supervisory work on readiness for the operational resilience expectations effective **1 September 2026**, and targeted work on third-party risk management.

**Lesson:** B-13, E-21 and B-10 are what supervisors test against. Keep the evidence ready.

cards.title: Stage 5 take-aways
items: E-21 separates operational risk management from operational resilience; full adherence was expected by 1 September 2026.
Banks identify critical operations, map dependencies, set tolerances for disruption and test severe but plausible scenarios.
E-21 expects staff training on operational risk and resilience, on continuity plans and their activation, and for people managing data.
B-10 covers every third-party arrangement across its life cycle, scaled to risk; the bank stays accountable.
Readiness means named owners, training and test records, OSFI incident reports, the PIPEDA breach record and tracked remediation.

cards.prompt: Which critical operation does your work support? If it stopped for a day, what would you do in the first hour, and where is your team's continuity plan?

quiz.question: How does E-21 define operational resilience?
options: The absence of any operational loss during the financial year
The risk of loss resulting from people, inadequate processes and systems, or from external events
The bank's insurance cover against cyber and technology failure
The ability to deliver operations, especially critical operations, through disruption
quiz.explanation: E-21 defines operational resilience as the ability to deliver operations, especially critical ones, through disruption. The risk of loss from people, processes and systems is the definition of operational risk.

quiz.question: Which E-21 section expects business and central functions to provide adequate training to staff on operational risk management and resilience?
options: Section 2.4.2
Section 1.2
Section 4.4
Section 3.3
quiz.explanation: Section 1.2 lists the duties of business and central functions, including adequate staff training on operational risk management and resilience. 3.3 covers scenario testing, 4.4 change management and 2.4.2 reporting.

quiz.question: What does E-21 section 4.1.2 expect regarding staff and business continuity plans?
options: Staff are trained on the plans only after a real disruption has occurred, so that the lessons are fresh and practical
Staff are trained on the plans, including activation and running operations in disruption
Only the crisis management team needs to read the plans
Plans are kept confidential from staff to prevent leaks
quiz.explanation: Section 4.1.2 says staff should be trained on business continuity plans, including their activation and how operations will be managed during disruption. Testing under 4.1.3 then builds understanding of roles.

quiz.question: How does E-21 distinguish tolerance for disruption from risk appetite?
options: Tolerance is the maximum disruption the bank can withstand in a crisis; appetite is risk it willingly accepts for business goals
They are the same measure under two different names
Tolerance applies only to cyber incidents and appetite only to credit
Appetite is set by OSFI while tolerance is set by the board
quiz.explanation: E-21 says tolerances differ from and are typically greater than risk appetite: appetite is risk willingly accepted, tolerance is the maximum disruption the bank can withstand. Operational risk limits are usually set below tolerances.

quiz.question: Marc-André's team maps the retail payments operation. What should the mapping consider under E-21?
options: Only the core banking software and its hardware
People, technology, processes, information, facilities, third parties and the links between them
Only third parties located outside Canada
Only the staff who work in the payments department
quiz.explanation: E-21 section 3.1 says mapping should view critical operations end to end and consider people, technology, processes, information, facilities, third parties and their interconnections.

quiz.question: Which of these is an example of a severe but plausible scenario that E-21 lists for scenario testing?
options: A critical third-party service disruption
A planned office redecoration
A routine monthly password change
A scheduled public holiday closure
quiz.explanation: E-21 section 3.3 gives power outages, large-scale technology failures, critical third-party disruptions, cyber incidents, natural disasters and pandemics as examples.

quiz.question: Under B-10, what happens to the bank's accountability when it outsources a service to a third party?
options: The bank keeps accountability for the outsourced activity and manages the risks
Accountability moves fully to the third party once the contract assigns the service and its risks to that party
Accountability ends once the contract is signed by legal counsel
Accountability is shared equally with OSFI
quiz.explanation: B-10's first principle says the institution is ultimately accountable for managing risks from all third-party arrangements and retains accountability for outsourced activities.

quiz.question: Which E-21 expectation applies to people responsible for managing and overseeing data?
options: They must hold a government security clearance issued before they are given access to any critical data
They are exempt from operational risk training
They must report every data change to OSFI
The data risk management program should include training programs for them
quiz.explanation: E-21 section 4.7 says the data risk management program should include training programs for the people responsible for managing and overseeing data, along with breach escalation and response processes.

quiz.question: A vendor's standard contract lacks audit rights and incident notice. Which B-10 expectation does this most directly miss?
options: Written agreements that set out rights and duties, including audit and incident notification
The need for the vendor to be a Canadian company
The need for OSFI to approve each vendor in advance
The need to pay vendors only after an annual audit
quiz.explanation: B-10 expects written agreements setting out each party's rights and responsibilities, including the right to audit and provisions that let the bank meet OSFI's incident reporting. It does not require OSFI pre-approval of vendors.

quiz.question: Who provides independent assurance under E-21 that operational risk controls, policies and systems are designed and operating effectively?
options: Internal audit or a similar function
The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre
The business line that owns the process
The vendor that supplies the system
quiz.explanation: E-21 section 1.4 gives that role to internal audit or a similar function, reporting to senior management and the board. Business lines own and manage risk; they cannot assure themselves independently.

regulators: Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI)
Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (OPC)
